title: Mughal-era India: bounded orientation for a parent chapter plan
evidence_status: Limited primary-institutional orientation excerpts, not completed chapter research

sources.title: South Asia 1400–1600
excerpts: Ibrahim II (of the Afghan Lodi sultanate based in Delhi) is defeated by Babur (Timur’s successor) in the Battle of Panipat, inaugurating the rule of the [Mughal dynasty](/toah/hd/mugh/hd_mugh.htm). From 1540 to 1555, Mughal control is lost to Afghan forces under Shir Shah Sur. After retreating to Persia, Humayun and his son Akbar reconquer the northern plains of South Asia and reestablish Mughal political dominance. At its height, the Mughal empire controls all of the northern subcontinent, from Bengal to Kabul to the Deccan.

Akbar succeeds to the throne after the death of Humayun. He establishes an effective and comprehensive administrative system for the Mughal empire, and adopts a policy of tolerance toward local religious beliefs. His atelier of artists is influenced by local as well as imported traditions, experimenting with Persian painting styles, in dialogue with Jain, Hindu, and Sultanate styles, to create a unique “Mughal style.”

sources.title: The Shah Jahan Album
excerpts: The album was initiated by the [Mughal](/toah/hd/mugh_2/hd_mugh_2.htm) emperor Jahangir (r. 1605–27), and passed onto his son Shah Jahan (r. 1628–58), who added several paintings, illuminations, and [calligraphy](/toah/hd/cali/hd_cali.htm) folios. It eventually came into the possession of Shah Jahan’s son Aurangzeb (r. 1658–1707). Little is believed to have been added by this final imperial patron, but the presence of his seal on one folio confirms that he was once the owner. Finally, around 1820, eleven more folios were added and the album was rebound. The added pages were completed in a style imitative of the seventeenth-century Mughal paintings and are characterized by a degree of stiffness and flatness of form. Thus, the album as it stands today is a collection of folios produced from the seventeenth through the [nineteenth](/toah/hd/irmd/hd_irmd.htm) centuries.

sources.title: The Art of the Mughals after 1600
excerpts: Jahangir’s successor [Shah Jahan](https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/empe/hd_empe.htm) (r. 1628–58) is most celebrated for his architectural achievements, the [Taj Mahal](http://dev-met-timeline.pantheon.io/nonmet/mugh_2_1/) being his (and perhaps the country’s) best known monument. He commissioned this tomb for his wife after her death in 1631 and it took sixteen years to complete. The building is set on the bank of the Jumna River in Agra with a formal eightfold garden and reflecting pools in front, its elevation of inlaid white marble striking against the red sandstone of the other buildings in the complex. After moving the capital from Agra to Delhi in 1648, Shah Jahan built a new city there, called Shahjahanabad, and a congregational mosque (1650–56), the largest in all of India. Paintings from his reign were characterized by formal portraits and courtly scenes, replacing the more wide-ranging and personal subject matter under Jahangir. The major commission of his reign was a history called the _Padshahnama_, illustrated through the 1640s.

Shah Jahan’s rule was forcibly terminated by his son in 1658. Aurangzeb (r. 1658–1707) held increasingly orthodox Sunni beliefs, and his reign saw the decline of Mughal patronage of the arts. Early portraits of him do exist, and he commissioned some notable architectural projects such as the Pearl Mosque (in the [Red Fort at Delhi](http://dev-met-timeline.pantheon.io/nonmet/mugh_2_2/)), but in 1680 he banned music and painting from his court. The emperors who followed him were too weak and the state too poor to support the production of sumptuous paintings and books as before; under Bahadur Shah (r. 1707–12) and Muhammad Shah (r. 1719–48), there was a slight resurgence in the arts, but the 1739 raid of Delhi by Nadir Shah caused much of the city’s population to flee and the artistic community to be permanently dispersed. By the 1800s, the Mughals were nominally still emperors of India, but under the protection of the British.

The reduction of artists in the Mughal painting workshops by Jahangir, Shah Jahan, and Aurangzeb meant that a number of artists had to find new work, and many regional courts benefited greatly from the influx of former imperial employees. Painting at the [Hindu Rajasthani courts](https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/rajp/hd_rajp.htm) such as Bikaner, Bundi, and Kota, and at the provincial Muslim courts of Lucknow, Murshidabad, Faizabad, and Farrukhabad, were all transformed as Mughal artists provided fresh inspiration. Among the important subimperial patrons of the early period was ‘Abd al-Rahim Muhammad Khan-i Khanan (1561–1626/27), commander-in-chief of the Mughal armies under both Akbar and Jahangir. A copy of the epic _Ramayana_ (1597–1605)—with 130 illustrations (2008.359.23) —and six other manuscripts can be attributed to his atelier.

sources.title: Desiring Landscapes: Avadh
excerpts: «In the permanent collection of the [Department of Islamic Art](/about-the-museum/museum-departments/curatorial-departments/islamic-art) are two miniature paintings from Avadh (Oudh), India. Avadh, located in the northeastern province of Uttar Pradesh, was once ruled by the Nawabs of Avadh (1722–1856), a group that gained autonomy during the disintegration of the Mughal Empire. Quickly, the Nawabs and their courtiers had to contend with the rise of the East India Company. After a decisive victory in the Battle of Buxar in 1764, the East India Company used Avadh as an effective buffer state against encroaching powers such as the Marathas and the Rohillas.»

The art of Avadh underscores this complicated, connected history, with Avadhi miniature painting in particular characterized as eclectic, weaving a hybrid of Persianate, Mughal, Indic, and European visual vocabularies. A testament to the interregional dialogue occurring in South Asia at the time, Avadhi miniatures drew from a variety of painting techniques and were overall invested in the depiction of "light and shadows and a more accurate rendition of volume and space" (Losty, 2011). Mihr Chand, Nidha Mal, Mir Kalan Khan, and Muhammad Faqirullah Khan are the most cited and celebrated artists who worked in and around Avadh. Many of them migrated to cities within Avadh, such as Faizabad and Lucknow, after the ruler of Persia, Nadir Shah, sacked Delhi and devastated the Mughal army in 1739. At this juncture, there was an enmeshed network of artistic patronage spurred by courtly elites and also by European traders. Indeed, foreigners like Richard Johnson, Jean-Baptiste-Joseph Gentil, and Colonel Antoine-Louis Henri Polier collected and even commissioned complete painting albums.

sources.title: Mughal Court and Art of Observation
excerpts: The Mughal dynasty (1526–1858) was among the richest and longest ruling in India, and at its peak controlled large portions of the Indian subcontinent.

sources.title: Armies of the East India Company
excerpts: The Company became India’s dominant power following victories at the Battles of [Plassey](/explore/battle-plassey) (1757), Wandewash (1760) and Buxar (1764). Its supremacy was confirmed in 1765, when it secured from the weak Mughal Emperor the right to gather tax and customs duties in Bengal, India’s richest province.

The Company’s mismanagement of India contributed to the outbreak of the [Indian Mutiny](/explore/why-did-indian-mutiny-happen) (1857-59), an uprising of Indian soldiers against their British commanders. Native rulers and thousands of ordinary people joined in this struggle that threatened to destroy British colonial power on the subcontinent.

sources.title: Bahadur Shah in exile
excerpts: Bahadur Shah Zafar (1775-1862) was the last Mughal Emperor of India, contemptuously dubbed the 'King or Emperor of Delhi' by the British. He is shown here in exile in Burma in the aftermath of the Indian Mutiny (1857-1859). Although there were calls for his execution, a promise had been made on his surrender that his life would be spared. Most of his sons suffered a worse fate; after they had surrendered the British killed them in cold blood.

anchors.claim: Babur defeated the Delhi Lodi ruler at Panipat in 1526, beginning Mughal rule.
Mughal control was interrupted by the Afghan Sur regime from 1540 to 1555; Humayun restored Mughal dominance after exile.
Akbar ruled from 1556 to 1605 and built an administrative system with policies of religious tolerance.
Mughal cultural production drew on Persian and local Indian traditions; cultural exchange belongs alongside political history.
Jahangir ruled in 1605–1627 and Shah Jahan in 1628–1658; their court art and Shah Jahan’s architecture provide distinct cultural contexts.
Shah Jahan was displaced in 1658; Aurangzeb ruled in 1658–1707. Do not turn an event-grounded mood into a hero/villain label.
Artists and patrons also worked at regional courts; later imperial weakening did not mean the disappearance of cultural production.
Nadir Shah’s raid on Delhi in 1739 disrupted the city and dispersed members of its artistic community.
The Nawabs of Avadh gained autonomy as Mughal political control weakened and interacted with the rising East India Company; regional agency matters.
Company victories at Plassey in 1757 and Buxar in 1764 preceded its acquisition of Bengal revenue rights from the Mughal emperor in 1765.
By the nineteenth century the Mughals remained nominal emperors under British protection; distinguish symbolic legitimacy from territorial government.
Bahadur Shah Zafar was the final Mughal emperor and was exiled after the 1857 uprising. The dynasty’s formal terminal date is 1858, beyond this film’s requested 1857 endpoint.

coverage_requirements: Founding and restored rule, not an unbroken empire from 1526 onward.
Explain institutions, alliances, revenue and ordinary people as well as rulers and monuments; unsupported specifics become explicit chapter research questions.
Give Aurangzeb-era expansion and political strains proper later research; an arts-focused brief cannot establish a single cause of imperial decline.
Represent regional states and changing cultural patronage as actors, not merely an empty interval between Mughal power and British rule.
Finish the political narrative at 1857 with a qualified note that formal abolition and exile belong to the aftermath, rather than misdating them.
cautions: Most early sources focus on art; additional chapter research is needed for the economy, peasant life, military institutions, women, the Deccan and regional politics.
Some museum descriptions contain sweeping characterizations of religion or declining court wealth. Do not generalize them into a sole explanation of political change.
Use neutral language such as uprising or rebellion for 1857; preserve source context without inheriting colonial terminology as the narrative voice.
Do not conflate Shah Jahan’s 1628 accession with a 1627 reign date found in some timelines, or Bahadur Shah I with Bahadur Shah Zafar.
Mood follows events and explanatory purpose; a prosperous court is not proof of universal prosperity.
